_meta.description: Equipment-sizing basis for the Evaluate BOM (backend/app/evaluate/bom.py): unit sizes used to turn MW/MWh into equipment counts for a ~1 GW AI data-center campus with on-site solar, wind, gas and batteries, a 230 kV interconnection and a 34.5 kV collector system. Equipment is described generically; datasheet URLs are cited only as evidence. PV ILR, wind-turbine rating, CC block and CT unit size are NOT here: they come from atb_2025_catalog.json. Every value is a representative 2027 design choice backed by the quoted source, not a vendor selection.

pv_module_w.source: Manufacturer datasheet: 530-550 W, 144 half-cut-cell bifacial mono-PERC dual-glass utility module, US-assembled (datasheet Ver2.5, January 2026)
pv_module_w.note: The brief sets 550 W. The datasheet title is '530-550 Watt Dual Glass Module 144 Half Cut Bifacial Monocrystalline PERC'. Its STC table ('Irradiance 1000 W/m², cell temperature 25 °C, AM 1.5') lists Pmax 530/535/540/545/550 W. The 550 W bin is: Vmp 41.96 V, Imp 13.11 A, Voc 49.90 V, Isc 14.00 A, 'Module Efficiency' 21.3%. Other rows: 'No. of Cells 144 (6 × 24)', 'Dimensions 2278 × 1134 × 30mm', 'Max. System Voltage DC 1500V (IEC/UL)', 'Power Tolerance (W) 0 ~ +5'. The rear-side gain is listed separately ('Rearside Power Gain (Reference to 550W Front)': 5%/15%/25% -> 578/633/688 W) and is NOT counted. The BOM uses the front-side STC nameplate, which is the DC (MWdc) basis of the ATB DC/AC ratio: modules = ceil(MWac * ILR * 1e6 / 550). Why this is representative for 2027: it is a current (2026-dated) 1,500 V bifacial c-Si module from a US assembly line with domestic-content cells. The LBNL 'U.S. Utility-Scale Solar, 2025 Data Update' slides (https://emp.lbl.gov/sites/default/files/2025-10/Utility%20Scale%20Solar%202025%20Edition%20Slides.pdf) say '99% of new project capacity chose single-axis tracking over fixed-tilt racking' and that 'c-Si modules expanded their market share in 2024 to 79% of newly installed capacity', so c-Si on trackers is the mainstream build. Caveat: higher-wattage modules would lower the count in proportion (count scales with 550/W); 550 W errs toward more modules.
pv_module_w.verification_note: Re-downloaded the cited datasheet PDF (footer 'AA550US-6x24GG-Ver2.5 (January 2026)'). Confirmed the STC row for the 550 W bin (Vmp 41.96 V, Imp 13.11 A, Voc 49.90 V, Isc 14.00 A, 21.3%), 'No. of Cells 144 (6×24)', '2278 × 1134 × 30mm', 'DC 1500V (IEC/UL)', power tolerance '0 ~ +5' and the rear-gain row 578/633/688 W. Efficiency recomputed: 550 / (2.278 × 1.134 m² × 1000 W/m²) = 21.3%. Both LBNL quotes found on slides 25-26 of the October 2025 '2025 Data Update' deck. 550 W is the brief's fixed value. It is a PERC-class rating, so newer higher-wattage modules would mean fewer modules (the note already says so).

pv_inverter_mva.units: MVA (AC) per central inverter / MV power-station skid
pv_inverter_mva.source: Manufacturer datasheet: 1,500 VDC central-inverter medium-voltage power station (inverter + MV transformer + MV switchgear on a 20-ft skid), 4,000/4,200/4,400/4,600 kVA US family, 'Last revised: 05/2025'
pv_inverter_mva.note: Datasheet rows for the largest model: 'Rated power with [PV inverter] (at -25°C to +35°C / 40°C optional 50°C) ... 4600 kVA / 4140 kVA'. Other rows: 'Typical nominal AC voltages 12 kV to 34.5 kV' and 'Max. input voltage 1500 V'. The skid is 'Delivered pre-configured on a 20-foot container-integrated skid' with 'Fully integrated transformer and switchgear'. Each inverter therefore carries its own MV step-up transformer, so the BOM's 'MV pad-mount step-up transformer, one per PV inverter' matches this skid's built-in transformer. The 4.6 MVA nameplate (at <=35 °C) is used because ATB PV MWac is an inverter-nameplate AC basis: inverters = ceil(MWac / 4.6). Caveats: (1) The datasheet's second figure, 4,140 kVA, is the rating at its higher-temperature point, labeled '40°C optional 50°C'. Kern County summer derating is not modeled. (2) At the 0.95 power factor required at the high side of the generator substation (see power_factor), full-kVA real output is 4.6 * 0.95 = 4.37 MW. Why this is representative for 2027: the datasheet offers a 4.0-4.6 MVA single-skid range at 34.5 kV and was revised in 2025, which matches the ~4-5 MVA utility central-inverter class.
pv_inverter_mva.verification_note: Re-downloaded the datasheet PDF ('Last revised: 05/2025', page 3). Confirmed the PV-inverter row '4600 kVA / 4140 kVA' at '-25°C to +35°C / 40°C optional 50°C', 'Typical nominal AC voltages 12 kV to 34.5 kV', 'Max. input voltage 1500 V', 'Delivered pre-configured on a 20-foot container-integrated skid' and 'Fully integrated transformer and switchgear'. Corrected the derating wording: the datasheet labels the 4,140 kVA point '40°C optional 50°C', not simply 50 °C.

bess_pcs_mw.units: MW real power per battery PCS / MV skid (4.6 MVA at 0.95 power factor)
bess_pcs_mw.source: Same 1,500 VDC medium-voltage power-station datasheet (storage-inverter variants, rev. 05/2025); real power derived at the 0.95 interconnection power factor
bess_pcs_mw.note: Datasheet rows for the 4,600 kVA station (page 3): 'Rated power with [newer storage-inverter variant] (from -25°C to +35°C / 40°C; optional 50°C) ... 4600 kVA / 4140 kVA*' (the asterisk means 'Preliminary'), and 'Discharging power with [extended-discharge storage variant] (at -25°C to + 25°C / 40°C optional 50°C) ... 4600 kVA / 3910 kVA' (no preliminary mark). The established storage variant is lower: 'Rated power with [standard storage inverter] (at -25°C to +25°C / 40°C optional 50°C) ... 3960 kVA / 3365 kVA'. The station is 'Ideally suited for PV applications, PV plus storage (DC coupled) and storage applications (AC coupled)'. Derivation: 4.6 MVA * 0.95 power factor (FERC Order 827 and CAISO Tariff 25.4.1, see power_factor) = 4.37 MW of real power while still supplying the required reactive range. BOM: PCS units = ceil(battery MW / 4.37), each with its own integrated MV step-up transformer. The power factor is applied to battery PCS but not to PV inverters on purpose: ATB PV MWac is already an inverter-nameplate AC rating, while battery MW is treated as real output at the 0.95 power factor. Caveats: the 4.6 MVA storage ratings hold only up to 35 °C (newer variant, preliminary) or 25 °C (extended-discharge variant) and fall at the higher-temperature point (4,140 / 3,910 kVA), which is not modeled. On the established 3.96 MVA variant, the value would be 3.96 * 0.95 = 3.76 MW, about 16% more PCS units. Why this is representative for 2027: it is the same 4-5 MVA, 34.5 kV skid class used for PV, so PV and storage share one MV design.
bess_pcs_mw.verification_note: Confirmed all three storage rows on page 3 of the re-downloaded datasheet. Corrected the note: the 4,600 kVA rated-power variant is a newer, preliminary one, not the 'standard' variant (the standard storage variant is 3,960 kVA at up to 25 °C). The 4,600 kVA figure is also given, without the preliminary mark, as the discharging power of the extended-discharge variant. Recomputed 4.6 × 0.95 = 4.37 MW.

battery_container_mwh.units: MWh (nameplate DC energy) per 20-ft BESS container
battery_container_mwh.source: Manufacturer datasheet: 20-ft liquid-cooled LFP (314 Ah cell) battery energy storage container for North America, 5,016 kWh (datasheet 2024/03)
battery_container_mwh.note: Datasheet rows: 'Battery cell LFP 314Ah', 'Battery configuration 12P416S', 'Battery capacity 5016 kWh', 'Rated voltage 1331.2 V', 'Maximum power 2508 kW', 'Cooling method Liquid cooling', 'Dimensions (W × H × D) ... (6058 × 2896 × 2438 mm)', 'Weight 94798.8 lb / 43 T', 'Compliance UL1973 / UL9540A / UL9540'. Key feature listed: 'High energy density: 5 MWh in one 20 ft container'. 5,016 kWh is rounded to 5.0 MWh. BOM: containers = ceil(battery MWh / 5.0). Cross-check: 314 Ah × 3.2 V (LFP nominal; 'Rated voltage 1331.2 V' / 416 cells in series) × 416 × 12 = 5,016 kWh. The datasheet's 'Maximum power 2508 kW' is 0.5C, so one container delivers at most ~2.5 MW. Durations under 2 h would be power-limited, which does not affect ATB's 2-10 h configurations. Caveat: this counts nameplate DC energy with no overbuild for depth-of-discharge limits, auxiliary load, round-trip losses or augmentation. Sizing on usable energy at the POI would need more containers. Why this is representative for 2027: the 314 Ah-cell, ~5 MWh, 20-ft liquid-cooled LFP container is the mainstream utility product class of 2024-2026 (search results this session showed several vendors offering the same 5.0 MWh/314 Ah/20-ft class; only this datasheet was opened). Denser 20-ft products are already announced: a 2024-04-09 announcement says a 20-ft LFP system 'achieves an impressive 6.25 MWh capacity in the TEU container' (https://www.catl.com/en/news/6232.html). If such units are standard by 2027, the container count falls by about 20% (5.0/6.25).
battery_container_mwh.verification_note: The cited PDF returned an empty reply to curl, so it was fetched with WebFetch. Its bytes are identical (SHA-1 f9e54a5f...) to the researcher's copy. Confirmed 'Battery cell LFP 314Ah', 'Battery configuration 12P416S', 'Battery capacity 5016 kWh', 'Rated voltage 1331.2 V', 'Maximum power 2508 kW', 'Liquid cooling', '19.88 × 9.50 × 8.00 ft (6058 × 2896 × 2438 mm)' (a 20-ft box, not 40-ft), '94798.8 lb / 43 T', 'UL1973 / UL9540A / UL9540', '5 MWh in one 20 ft container' and '2024/03-MKT NA'. Recomputed 314 Ah × 3.2 V × 416 × 12 = 5,016 kWh. The 6.25 MWh 20-ft passage is confirmed on the April 9, 2024 announcement page.

power_factor.units: dimensionless (real/apparent power) used to convert MW to MVA for transformer and MV sizing
power_factor.source: FERC Order No. 827, Reactive Power Requirements for Non-Synchronous Generation, 155 FERC ¶ 61,277, Docket RM16-1-000 (issued June 16, 2016): pro forma LGIA reactive-power requirement; same range in the CAISO tariff, Section 25.4.1
power_factor.note: P 1: 'newly interconnecting non-synchronous generators ... will be required to provide dynamic reactive power within the range of 0.95 leading to 0.95 lagging at the high-side of the generator substation.' The pro forma LGIA text: 'Interconnection Customer shall design the Large Generating Facility to maintain a composite power delivery at continuous rated power output at the high-side of the generator substation at a power factor within the range of 0.95 leading to 0.95 lagging, unless the Transmission Provider has established a different power factor range that applies to all non-synchronous generators in the Control Area on a comparable basis.' For synchronous units (on-site gas), the existing LGIA requires 'continuous rated power output at the Point of Interconnection at a power factor within the range of 0.95 leading to 0.95 lagging' (P 3, from Order No. 2003). BOM use: MVA = MW / 0.95 for the main power transformers, data-center service transformers, unit substations and MV feeders. CAISO's own tariff uses the same range: Fifth Replacement Electronic Tariff, Section 25.4.1 'Asynchronous Generating Facilities-Reactive Power' (version as of August 5, 2026; https://www.caiso.com/documents/section-25-interconnection-of-generating-units-and-facilities-as-of-aug-05-2026.pdf): '... will maintain a composite power delivery at continuous rated power output at the high-side of the generator substation at a power factor within the range of 0.95 leading to 0.95 lagging, unless the CAISO has established a different power factor range that applies to all Asynchronous Generating Facilities on a comparable basis.' That section covers existing facilities that replace units; new-facility technical requirements are in Appendix H to Appendix LL, which was not opened. Why this is representative for 2027: it is still the FERC pro forma default and the CAISO tariff text in force in 2026. Caveat: PG&E interconnection handbooks were not checked.
power_factor.verification_note: Re-downloaded FERC Order No. 827 (155 FERC ¶ 61,277, Docket RM16-1-000, 'Issued June 16, 2016'). Confirmed verbatim the P 1 summary sentence, the new pro forma LGIA text (page 6) and the existing-LGIA quote in P 3 (page 7). Added the CAISO tariff §25.4.1 text (August 5, 2026 version), which uses the same 0.95 leading/lagging range at the high side of the generator substation.

mpt_mva.units: MVA per main power transformer (230/34.5 kV, top fan-cooled rating)
mpt_mva.source: Transformer-manufacturer catalog (collector step-up class for solar/wind/BESS: '45 MVA up to 500 MVA'; utility and data-center substation class: 'Up to 200 MVA', 34.5 kV-class LV, up to 230 kV-class HV), cross-checked against 230/34.5 kV renewable-project filings
mpt_mva.note: The same maker's catalog lists two relevant classes. (a) Collector step-up transformers for solar, wind and BESS plants, the generator-side class an MPT belongs to (this URL): 'Ratings: 45 MVA up to 500 MVA (North American facilities)' and 'Voltage: Up to 550kV (North American facilities)'. (b) Utility and data-center step-down substation transformers (https://www.prolec.energy/transformers/power-transformers/substation-transformers/): 'Typical Ratings Up to 200 MVA Low voltage: 15 kV class to 34.5 kV class – wye connection High voltage: 34.5 kV class to 230 kV class – delta or wye connection'. Class (b) serves load, not generation. It is cited only to show that 230/34.5 kV windings at up to 200 MVA are a standard catalog range. Built 230/34.5 kV examples: (1) SPP GEN-2017-239, a 300 MW solar project: 'Two 230/34.5 kV 100/133/167 MVA (ONAN/ONAF/ONAF) step-up transformer' (https://opsportal.spp.org/documents/studies/files/2017_Generation_Studies/GEN-2017-239%20IFS%20Summary%20Draft.pdf). (2) A 270 MW southern-California solar project with a 230 kV tie: 'two (2) ... 34.5 kV, 84/112/140 MVA station transformers' (https://eciusa.com/projects/mccoy-solar-34-5-kv-collection-system/). (3) A 2011 Ontario wind+solar park: 'The wind power transformer is rated 100/133/166 MVA while the solar power transformer is rated 65/86/108 MVA' (https://patternenergy.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/GRW-Project_Description_Report_01Jul11.pdf). Choice: 200 MVA, inside the 45-500 MVA collector step-up range and above the 140-167 MVA top ratings of the built examples, because a multi-GW on-site fleet favors large units. The 34.5 kV LV current limits the size: 200e6 / (sqrt(3) * 34.5e3) = 3,347 A. That exceeds one 3,000 A-class 38 kV main breaker (see mv_feeders_per_switchgear_lineup), so each MPT feeds two 34.5 kV bus sections. The value is treated as the top (fan-cooled) rating, as the project examples quote it. BOM: MPTs = ceil(on-site nameplate MW incl. battery / 0.95 / 200). Caveats: (1) Using the documented 167 MVA size instead raises the count by about 20%. (2) On-site gas turbines step up through their own GSUs (one per turbine in bom.py). If 'on-site nameplate MW' includes gas, that MW would be counted twice, so only the inverter-based PV, wind and battery MW should go through the 34.5 kV MPTs.
mpt_mva.verification_note: Confirmed on the re-downloaded pages: the catalog's 'Up to 200 MVA ... 34.5 kV class to 230 kV class' row, which sits under 'Utility & Data Center Transformers', a step-down class; the collector step-up page's '45 MVA up to 500 MVA'; SPP GEN-2017-239 (published April 2023), 'Two 230/34.5 kV 100/133/167 MVA (ONAN/ONAF/ONAF)' for 300 MW; the 270 MW, 230 kV solar project's '84/112/140 MVA station transformers' (the page prints '3034.5 kV'); and the July 2011 draft park report's '100/133/166 MVA' and '65/86/108 MVA'. Corrected the class label: the researcher called the 200 MVA row the top of the 34.5 kV generator class, but it belongs to the step-down class, so the collector step-up page is now the primary URL. Recomputed the LV current: 3,347 A. 200 MVA is kept as a realistic large unit.

mv_feeder_mw.units: MW per 34.5 kV collector / distribution feeder
mv_feeder_mw.source: Built 34.5 kV collector systems (engineering-firm project pages, developer project report) and 34.5 kV-class switchgear ratings
mv_feeder_mw.note: Evidence: (1) A 270 MW solar project ('total capacity at full generation of 270 MW') with six overhead feeders north plus two east, i.e. 8 feeders = 33.75 MW per feeder, using cable that 'varied from 1250 to 500 kcmil'. (2) A 345/34.5 kV PV collector substation: 'PV Substation – 200 MVA, Two 345/34.5kV transformers, Three 345kV SF6 breakers, Seven MV collection feeder breakers arranged on two buses', about 28.6 MVA per feeder (https://bodecinc.com/project/345kv-pv-collector-substation-with-t-line-epc/). (3) A 2011 park report: 'The power output from each of the 1 MW SSUs (100 MW in total) is connected via 5 underground 34.5 kV power cable circuits', i.e. 20 MW per circuit (https://patternenergy.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/09/GRW-Project_Description_Report_01Jul11.pdf). 30 MW at 0.95 power factor = 31.6 MVA = 529 A at 34.5 kV. That is well inside 34.5 kV-class feeder breakers ('1200A, 2000A Rated Current (A)', 2025 38 kV metal-clad switchgear product sheet: https://www.iemfg.com/system/uploads/fae/file/asset/65/IEM-ProductSheet-MV-38KVSwitchgear-20250402.pdf) and the '600 A / 800 A' MV-switchgear options on the PV/BESS skids (pv_inverter_mva source). In practice derated cable ampacity and voltage drop set the limit (not modeled). The data-center side uses the same feeder size. BOM: feeders = ceil(on-site MW / 30) + ceil(peak MW / 30). Why this is representative for 2027: it sits mid-range of the 20-34 MW per-feeder values seen in built projects.
mv_feeder_mw.verification_note: Confirmed that the 270 MW project has eight 34.5 kV feeders (six north plus two east; 'four (4) collection 34.5kV feeder circuits connected to each transformer'; 270 / 8 = 33.75 MW) and cable that 'varied from 1250 to 500 kcmil'. Confirmed the 345/34.5 kV substation's '200 MVA ... Seven MV collection feeder breakers arranged on two buses' (28.6 MVA each), the 2011 report's '5 underground 34.5 kV power cable circuits' for 100 MW (20 MW each), the switchgear sheet's breaker row '1200A, 2000A Rated Current (A)' (sheet version 2025_01_03_Rev01), and the skid's '600 A / 800 A' MV-switchgear options. Recomputed 30 / 0.95 = 31.6 MVA, and 31.58e6 / (sqrt(3) × 34.5e3) = 528.5 A.

mv_feeders_per_switchgear_lineup.units: feeder breakers per 34.5 kV metal-clad switchgear lineup (one bus section)
mv_feeders_per_switchgear_lineup.source: Built 34.5 kV collector substations (4 feeders per transformer; 3.5 per bus), checked against 38 kV metal-clad breaker continuous-current ratings (1200/2000/3000 A)
mv_feeders_per_switchgear_lineup.note: Evidence: a 270 MW solar substation (two 84/112/140 MVA transformers, this URL) has 'four (4) collection 34.5kV feeder circuits connected to each transformer'. A 200 MVA PV substation has 'Seven MV collection feeder breakers arranged on two buses', i.e. 3.5 per bus (https://bodecinc.com/project/345kv-pv-collector-substation-with-t-line-epc/). Current check: four 30 MW feeders at 0.95 power factor = 4 × 31.6 MVA = 126 MVA = 2,114 A at 34.5 kV. A 38 kV metal-clad switchgear datasheet lists 'Rated Continuous Current (A) 1200/2000/3000' under 'Ratings – All Units – ANSI C37.06 & C37.09' (https://www.myerspower.com/literature/38kVSwitchgear-DataSheet.pdf). A 3,000 A-class main (sqrt(3) × 34.5 kV × 3,000 A = 179 MVA) therefore carries four feeders with margin; a 2,000 A main (119.5 MVA) would carry only 3.8. A second 38 kV product sheet (https://www.iemfg.com/system/uploads/fae/file/asset/65/IEM-ProductSheet-MV-38KVSwitchgear-20250402.pdf) gives 'Ampacity: 1200A' for the assembly and '1200A, 2000A Rated Current (A)' for its breakers, plus a 'Main-tie-main automatic transfer scheme'. Its 2,000 A is a breaker rating, not a bus rating. With 200 MVA main power transformers (3,347 A LV; 200 × 0.95 / 30 = 6.3 feeders at full rating), each transformer feeds two such lineups. A lineup = main breaker + 4 feeder breakers; tie, auxiliary and capacitor bays are not counted separately. BOM: lineups = ceil(feeders / 4).
mv_feeders_per_switchgear_lineup.verification_note: Corrected the derivation. The researcher read the product sheet's '1200A, 2000A Rated Current' as a 2,000 A bus, but those are breaker ratings, and the sheet's assembly 'Ampacity' is 1200A. The value 4 now rests on built substations (4 per transformer and 3.5 per bus, both quotes confirmed on re-downloaded pages) and on a second 38 kV datasheet I opened that lists 1200/2000/3000 A continuous ratings. Under a 3,000 A main, four 31.6 MVA feeders (2,114 A) fit. Value unchanged.

hv_breakers_per_element.units: HV (230 kV) circuit breakers per connected element (breaker-and-a-half bus)
hv_breakers_per_element.source: National Research Council (2012), Terrorism and the Electric Power Delivery System, Appendix F: Substation Configurations, National Academies Press, doi:10.17226/12050
hv_breakers_per_element.note: Appendix F, 'BREAKER-AND-A-HALF CONFIGURATION': 'The breaker-and-a-half configuration, typically used at extra-high-voltage (EHV) stations, consists of two buses, each normally energized. Electrically connected between the buses are three circuit breakers and, between each two breakers, a circuit ... In this arrangement, three circuit breakers are used in a bay for two independent circuits; hence, each circuit shares the common center circuit breaker, so there are 1.5 circuit breakers per circuit. The breaker-and-a-half configuration provides for circuit breaker maintenance, since any breaker can be removed from service and isolated without interrupting any circuit.' The same appendix on ring buses: 'For stations having three to five circuits, a ring bus is often used. As more circuits are added, the configuration may evolve to a breaker-and-a-half arrangement.' A small collector station shows the ring-bus end of that range: 'Three 345kV SF6 breakers' for two transformers plus one line (https://bodecinc.com/project/345kv-pv-collector-substation-with-t-line-epc/). An INL 2022 reliability study (https://www.osti.gov/servlets/purl/1968318) notes that the USDA RUS Bulletin 1724E-300 Design Guide for Rural Substations 'outlines six common substation configuration types ... single bus, sectionalized bus, operate/transfer, ring bus, breaker and a half, and double breaker/double bus'. Breaker-and-a-half was chosen (spec decision) because a 1 GW campus switchyard has many elements (main power transformers, service transformers, line terminals) that must be maintainable without outages. 230 kV is below EHV, so this is a conservative, high-reliability choice. BOM: HV breakers = ceil(1.5 * (MPTs + service transformers + line terminals)); ceil covers the 2-breaker last bay when the element count is odd.
hv_breakers_per_element.verification_note: Confirmed the breaker-and-a-half passage verbatim on the re-fetched NAP Appendix F page (doi:10.17226/12050), plus its ring-bus sentence (added). Confirmed the INL paper (INL/CON-22-66879, June 2022) passage on the six RUS 1724E-300 configurations. The bulletin itself was not opened.

dc_ups_module_mw.units: MW per large 3-phase data-center UPS module (480 V)
dc_ups_module_mw.source: Manufacturer product page: large 3-phase modular double-conversion UPS block, 1500 kVA/1500 kW, 480 V 3-wire, UL version, positioned for AI/HPC data centers
dc_ups_module_mw.note: Product page rows: 'Power Rating 1500kVA/1500kW', 'Input Voltage Range 480 (408 to 552) 3Ph+PE', 'Output Voltage Range 480 (408 to 552) 3Ph+PE', 'Efficiency ≥ 97% Double Conversion VFI ≥ 99% Dynamic Online Mode', 'Weight 3800 kgs'. Features: 'It delivers more power in a single block, ideal to support large-scale data centers for AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) applications' and 'From 1.5MW up to 20MW, this power solution can adapt to your system needs across power capacity, redundancy, and design.' BOM: UPS modules = ceil(IT MW / 1.5 * dc_ups_redundancy_factor), with IT MW = peak_mw / PUE. Why this is representative for 2027: it is a current-generation 1.5 MW single block marketed specifically for AI/HPC halls, and it is the building block of multi-MW lineups. Caveat: some AI designs move UPS to the rack or to medium voltage; that is not modeled.
dc_ups_module_mw.verification_note: Re-fetched the product page and confirmed 'Power Rating 1500kVA/1500kW', '480 (408 to 552) 3Ph+PE' input and output, the efficiency row, 'Weight 3800 kgs', 'It delivers more power in a single block, ideal to support large-scale data centers for AI and High-Performance Computing (HPC) applications' and 'From 1.5MW up to 20MW'. The page also lists 'Operating Temperature 0 to 50 with automatic derating from 40°C'.

dc_ups_redundancy_factor.units: installed UPS capacity / IT load (4-to-make-3 distributed redundant, 4N/3)
dc_ups_redundancy_factor.source: White Paper 75 rev. 4, 'Comparing UPS System Design Configurations' (K. McCarthy, EDG2 Inc.; V. Avelar), plus a 2021 data-center operator article on 4-to-make-3 distributed redundancy
dc_ups_redundancy_factor.note: White paper (copy hosted at the URL; the official download link is https://www.se.com/au/en/download/document/SPD_SADE-5TPL8X_EN/). Its table maps 'Distributed redundant 4 Tier III $24,000 - $30,000 / rack' and 'System plus system (2N, 2N+1) 5 = Highest Tier IV'. It says 'Distributed redundant configurations, also known as tri-redundant, are commonly used in the large data center market today especially within financial organizations' and 'Overall, distributed redundant systems are usually chosen for large multi-megawatt installations where concurrent maintenance is a requirement and space is limited. UPS module savings over a 2N architecture also drive this configuration.' The operator article (https://www.stackinfra.com/resources/thought-leadership/weighing-in-on-block-vs-distributed-redundancy/, 2021-01-26) says: 'The “four-to-make-three” (4M3) design automatically switches power distribution to the remaining systems — whether due to unplanned downtime or for cases of maintenance and repair — until full power distribution can be restored.' The same article on block redundancy: 'Like a 4M3 DRS, a block redundant system will also have four systems, but instead of using all four at once, three of them supply the primary power and one remains in reserve for failover.' So 4/3 also covers the 3+1 block-redundant design. The white paper's own tri-redundant example (Figure 6: three 150 kW UPS for 300 kW of load) is 3-make-2, a factor of 1.5. Factor: 4 systems each rated N/3 gives installed capacity = 4/3 * N (2N would be 2.0). Choice: 4/3, the concurrently maintainable (Tier III-class) multi-MW norm, which avoids 2N's 100% extra UPS. Set 2.0 to model a 2N (Tier IV-class) design. The same factor scales the MV/LV unit-substation count in bom.py.

dc_unit_substation_mva.units: MVA per MV/LV unit-substation transformer (34.5 kV-class primary to 480 V-class secondary)
dc_unit_substation_mva.source: Data-center electrical design references (2025-2026 fabricator and transformer-manufacturer technical articles) and DoD UFGS-26 11 16 'Secondary Unit Substations' (Nov 2021)
dc_unit_substation_mva.note: Fabricator article on the hyperscale power chain: 'From the MV switchgear, feeders run to unit substation transformers — often 2,500 to 3,750 kVA each, in dry-type or liquid-filled construction — that step the power down to utilization voltage. In a 2N building there are two independent sets of them, physically separated.' It also says 'Utility feed at medium voltage (34.5 or 13.8 kV) arrives from the campus substation'. Transformer-maker article dated October 2, 2025 (https://northfieldtransformers.com/blog/the-evolving-role-of-transformers-in-data-centers/): 'Medium-Voltage Transformers (1–5 MVA) distribute power across the campus, converting voltages to the 400–480 V range for IT and mechanical loads', and colocation providers 'typically deploy standardized 2.5 MVA dry-type units per hall'. UFGS-26 11 16 (https://nibs-s3-wbdg3-production.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com/FFC/DOD/UFGS/UFGS%2026%2011%2016.pdf) has an unit-substation transformer sound-level table that runs to 'kVA Range ... 3001-4000 ... 64' dB. 3.0 MVA is chosen inside the cited 2.5-3.75 MVA band. At 480 V that is 3.0e6 / (sqrt(3) * 480) = 3,608 A. The UFGS scope note covers 'three phase secondary unit substations for step-down operation at primary voltages of 601 volts through 38 kilovolts, and secondary voltages, of 600 volts or less', and for one command says 'do not use secondary unit substations with secondary current greater than 5000 amperes'. 3.0 MVA at 480 V (3,608 A) is within that limit; 3.75 MVA would be 4,511 A. BOM: unit substations = ceil(peak MW / 0.95 / 3.0) * dc_ups_redundancy_factor (bom.py should round the product up to a whole unit, since 4/3 times an integer is often fractional). Why this is representative for 2027: it is the middle of the band that current hyperscale references cite for 480 V-class halls.
dc_unit_substation_mva.verification_note: Confirmed both article passages and the October 2, 2025 date on re-fetched pages. In UFGS-26 11 16 (November 2021), confirmed the liquid-filled transformer sound-level table rows up to '3001-4000 64' and the scope note (601 V through 38 kV primary, 600 V or less secondary). Recomputed 3.0e6 / (sqrt(3) × 480) = 3,608 A. No manufacturer unit-substation catalog was opened, so the value is a band-midpoint assumption, as labeled.

dc_service_transformer_mva.units: MVA per HV/MV data-center service transformer (230 kV-class to 34.5 kV-class)
dc_service_transformer_mva.source: Transformer-manufacturer technical article (Oct 2025) and utility hyperscale-campus project reporting (Sept 2022), cross-checked against a transformer catalog's data-center class
dc_service_transformer_mva.note: Article (October 2, 2025): 'Large Power Transformers (tens to hundreds of MVA) connect campuses to the utility grid, stepping high-voltage transmission (115 kV–230 kV) down to 34.5 kV or 13.8 kV. Utilities now view 100 MVA transformers as standard for large campuses.' It also says a '225 MW Illinois campus required four 100 MVA transformers at a new substation.' Trade press on that project (https://www.renewableenergyworld.com/hydro-power/dams-civil-structures/comed-debuts-100mva-transformers-at-new-hyperscale-data-center/, 2022-09-13, read via a summarizing fetch, not a raw copy) says the utility is 'building a new substation that includes 100MVA transformers ...' to 'accommodate the 225 MW of power the site will need.' Catalog cross-check (https://www.prolec.energy/transformers/power-transformers/substation-transformers/): data-center transformers 'use utility substation transformers and technical specifications', with 'Typical Ratings Up to 200 MVA ... High voltage: 34.5 kV class to 230 kV class'. BOM: service transformers = ceil(peak MW / 0.95 / 100) + 1 (N+1), i.e. 11 + 1 = 12 for a 1,000 MW peak. Why this is representative for 2027: it is the standard utility campus size named in the 2025 source. A smaller standard unit than the 200 MVA class maximum also keeps the N+1 spare modest (a judgment, not sourced). Caveats: using 200 MVA units would give 6 + 1 = 7. The cited 225 MW campus installs four 100 MVA units (400 MVA against 225 / 0.95 = 237 MVA of peak, about 1.7×), which is more redundancy than N+1, so the BOM's N+1 count is lean.
dc_service_transformer_mva.verification_note: Confirmed on the re-fetched article (October 2, 2025): 'Utilities now view 100 MVA transformers as standard for large campuses' and the four 100 MVA units for a 225 MW campus. The trade-press page returned 403 to curl; a summarizing fetch confirmed 'building a new substation that includes 100MVA transformers', 'the first order of four devices' and '225 MW', dated September 13, 2022. Confirmed the catalog's data-center row. Recomputed 1000 / 0.95 / 100 = 10.5 → 11 + 1 = 12, and with 200 MVA, 5.3 → 6 + 1 = 7. Added that the cited campus used about 1.7× its peak MVA, more than N+1.
